extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners, patent attorneys/agents, and Office personnel
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing obviousness under 35 U.S.C. §103, with emphasis on chemical compounds (lead compound selection, predictability, 'obvious to try', use of known techniques, and treatment of secondary considerations). Intended to direct USPTO examiners how to articulate findings and apply case law (KSR, Federal Circuit decisions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve Graham factual inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries before applying any obviousness rationale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a prerequisite for each rationale described (e.g., lead compound, known technique, obvious-to-try). The remaining listed findings for each rationale are to be articulated after resolving Graham facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation of similar properties may suffice without explicit teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: An expectation of similar properties in light of the prior art can be sufficient to support obviousness even without an explicit teaching in the prior art to isolate or make the claimed compound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Aventis: requiring an explicit teaching to purify a stereoisomer is a rigid TSM-style requirement disfavored by KSR. Office personnel may rely on an expectation of similar properties derived from structural similarity or other prior art disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead compound selection requires a reason to start with that compound
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be some reason for starting with a particular lead compound other than the mere fact that the lead compound exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reason can come from many sources (structural similarity, taught properties, market pressures, examiner/experts' evidence). An inactive compound can nevertheless serve as a lead compound if there is a reason (even unrelated to pharmaceutical activity) to select and modify it (Altana, Eisai, Altana/Altana discussion). Mere existence of a prior art compound is insufficient (Altana Pharma AG v. Teva; Altana/Altana discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural similarity can provide the necessary motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness based on structural similarity can be proved by identification of some motivation that would have led one of ordinary skill to select and then modify a known compound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is sufficient to show that the claimed and prior art compounds possess a 'sufficiently close relationship ... to create an expectation, in light of the totality of the prior art, that the new compound will have similar properties' (Eisai). However, there still must be a reason to select and modify the prior art compound, and a reasonable expectation of success when required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Must articulate a reason to modify and a reasonable expectation of success
rubrics_metrics.description: To base an obviousness rejection on modification of a prior art compound, there must be both a reason to modify the starting compound and a reasonable expectation of success in achieving the claimed compound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procter & Gamble and other cases emphasize both prongs: (1) reason to select/modify (may be structural similarity, teachings about properties, market pressures), and (2) reasonable expectation that the routine modification would yield the claimed result. If modification would not have been routine or predictable, obviousness is weak (Procter & Gamble, risedronate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of secondary considerations (unexpected results, commercial success, long-felt need)
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary considerations can rebut a prima facie case of obviousness; courts evaluate unexpected results, commercial success, and long-felt but unsolved need as of the filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unexpected results should be shown by credible evidence (tests comparing claimed vs. prior art, witness testimony, weight and credibility of evidence). Commercial success and long-felt need must be evaluated as of the filing date; commercial success may be given little weight where competing products are owned by the same assignee (Procter & Gamble). Examiners should analyze such evidence in detail when presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Known Technique To Improve Similar Devices (Methods, or Products) in the Same Way — four required findings
rubrics_metrics.description: To reject a claim based on applying a known technique used to improve similar items in the same way, examiners must articulate: (1) a finding that the prior art contained a 'base' device (method, or product) upon which the claimed invention can be seen as an 'improvement'; (2) a finding that the prior art contained a 'comparable' device that has been improved in the same way as the claimed invention; (3) a finding that one of ordinary skill could have applied the known 'improvement' technique in the same way to the 'base' device and the results would have been predictable; and (4) whatever additional Graham factual findings are necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: a method of enhancing a class of devices has been made part of the ordinary capabilities of one skilled in the art based on its teaching in other situations. If any of these findings cannot be made, the rationale cannot support obviousness. (See Altana discussion and numbered list in the text.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying a Known Technique to a Known Device Ready for Improvement — four required findings
rubrics_metrics.description: To reject a claim on the basis that a known technique applied to a known device ready for improvement would yield predictable results, examiners must articulate: (1) the prior art contained a 'base' device that the claimed invention improves; (2) the prior art contained a known technique applicable to the base device; (3) one of ordinary skill would have recognized that applying the known technique would have yielded predictable results and produced the improved system; and (4) any additional Graham factual findings required by the case facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: the technique is part of the ordinary capabilities of the skilled artisan; if applying the technique would have been beyond ordinary skill, the rationale fails (KSR). Examples include Dann v. Johnston and In re Nilssen.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Obvious to try' — finite predictable solutions and reasonable expectation of success — four required findings
rubrics_metrics.description: To reject under an 'obvious to try' rationale, examiners must find: (1) at the time of the invention there was a recognized problem or need (including design need or market pressure); (2) a finite number of identified, predictable potential solutions to that problem; (3) a person of ordinary skill could have pursued the known potential solutions with a reasonable expectation of success; and (4) any additional Graham factual findings necessary to explain obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR endorses an 'obvious to try' rationale only when the number of options is finite and predictable and there is a reasonable expectation of success. Courts emphasize predictability and reasonable expectations, particularly in chemical arts (Pfizer — finite set of pharmaceutically acceptable salts; Alza — predictable absorption properties; Kubin — routine methods to isolate nucleic acid). Examiners must articulate these findings and consider field-specific predictability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context-specific evaluation for 'obvious to try' and predictability
rubrics_metrics.description: The viability of an obvious-to-try argument depends on the particular field's characteristics, its state of advance, the nature of the known choices, the specificity or generality of the prior art, and the predictability of results in the area of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts caution that the evaluation must reflect how technical advance is achieved in the specific scientific or technical field (Abbott Labs. v. Sandoz). In unpredictable fields (e.g., certain chemical/biotech areas), an 'obvious to try' rationale is less likely to succeed unless predictability and reasonable expectation of success are shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictability and routine nature of modifications
rubrics_metrics.description: If the necessary modifications to a prior art compound or process would not have been routine or the result unpredictable, then a prima facie case of obviousness is weak or absent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several cases (Eisai, Procter & Gamble, In re Kubin, In re Urbanski) illustrate that unpredictability of results (potency, toxicity, reaction outcomes, biochemical sequence isolation) undercuts obviousness. Examiners should assess whether the modification would have been within ordinary skill and whether the result would have been predictable.
